issues.legal_issue: Repeated re-promulgation of temporary executive ordinances without legislative consideration is constitutionally invalid.
material_facts: A succession of ordinances was promulgated to continue the school takeover scheme, but none was replaced by legislation enacted by the state legislature.
The later ordinances repeated the earlier scheme and included provisions treating actions under the previous ordinance as actions under the new one.
issues.conclusion: Both judges agreed that the ordinances from the second ordinance onwards were invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Article 213(2) requires an ordinance to be laid before the legislature and limits its duration; Article 174 reinforces that ordinances are temporary. Re-promulgation cannot be used to let the executive exercise the legislature’s law-making role indefinitely. The court relied on Dr. D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar, which condemned routine successive re-promulgation without legislative consideration.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_repromulgate: A party challenges the constitutional validity of successive ordinances promulgated by the executive.
predicates.successive_repromulgation: The executive reissues ordinances to continue a scheme after earlier ordinances cease to operate.
predicates.no_legislative_enactment: The legislature does not enact the continued scheme into law.

issues.definition: When successive ordinances continue a scheme without legislative enactment, a constitutional challenge to them results in the later ordinances being invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The validity of an initial ordinance forming part of a succession of re-promulgated ordinances was disputed.
material_facts: The initial ordinance took over private schools and their assets without providing compensation to their owners.
Further ordinances continued the scheme without the legislature enacting it.
The state did not explain why the initial ordinance could not be placed before the legislature or establish that immediate action was required.
issues.conclusion: The judges disagreed: one considered the initial ordinance invalid as part of an unconstitutional chain and also arbitrary in taking private assets without compensation; the other considered it valid and distinct from the later invalid ordinances. The issue was referred to a larger bench.
issues.legal_principle: One opinion applied Article 213 and the reasoning in Dr. D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar to treat the ordinances as a connected course of executive action, and relied on Article 14 and C.B. Gautam v. Union of India for the uncompensated taking of private assets. The other opinion treated the initial ordinance as a valid exercise of the ordinance-making power and held that the later re-promulgations could be invalidated separately.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_initial_ordi: A party challenges the constitutional validity of an initial ordinance.
predicates.initial_ordinance_in_repromulgation_chai: The initial ordinance is followed by repeated ordinances continuing the same scheme without legislative enactment.
predicates.judicial_opinions_divided: The deciding judges reach opposing conclusions on the validity of the initial ordinance.

issues.definition: When an initial ordinance in a succession of re-promulgated ordinances is challenged and the judges disagree about its validity, that validity remains unresolved.

issues.legal_issue: The effect of an ordinance’s expiry on rights and government status created under it was disputed.
material_facts: The initial ordinance stated that qualifying school employees would become government employees and that the schools and their assets would vest in the state.
The ordinance expired without being replaced by an act of the legislature.
The state had not completed the contemplated inquiries or absorbed the employees, and the schools had not in fact been taken over under the later ordinances before the final ordinance expired.
issues.conclusion: The judges disagreed: one held that any status under the initial ordinance ended when it ceased to operate and that no government-employee rights survived; the other held that the initial ordinance created enduring vested rights, including government-employee status, which survived expiry unless reversed by legislation. The issue was referred to a larger bench.
issues.legal_principle: One opinion held that only irreversible completed effects of a temporary enactment may endure, relying on State of Orissa v. Bhupendra Kumar Bose, S. Krishnan v. State of Madras, T. Venkata Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, S.S. Dhanoa v. Union of India, and M.L. Kamra v. Chairman-cum-Managing Director, New India Assurance Co. Ltd. The other relied on Bhupendra Kumar Bose, T. Venkata Reddy, and Stevenson v. Oliver for the principle that enduring rights vested under a temporary enactment may survive its expiry.

predicates.proceeding_concerning_expired_ordinance: The case concerns rights said to have arisen under an ordinance that has ceased to operate.
predicates.ordinance_purported_to_create_employee_s: The ordinance stated that specified employees would become government employees.
predicates.judicial_opinions_divided: The deciding judges reach opposing conclusions on whether the asserted status survives expiry.

issues.definition: When an expired ordinance purported to create employee status and the judges disagree about whether that status survives, its survival remains unresolved.
